title: Two words for "to be"
goal: Master a distinction English doesn't make at all: when to use *ser* and when to use *estar* — and see that choosing the wrong one isn't just sloppy, it changes the meaning.
bekal: learn the forms of *estar* and set them side by side with *ser*
apply the dividing rule: built-in characteristics versus passing states
talk about your feelings and condition: *estou cansado*, *estou com fome*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Uma segunda-feira difícil
dialogs.intro: Monday morning in the course's waiting room. Carla sees Budi sitting there looking worn out.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Não, não estou doente. Só estou com sono.
lines.id: No, I'm not sick. I'm just sleepy.
lines.literal: no, not I-am(estar) sick. only I-am(estar) with sleep.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Ah, entendi. E a aula? É difícil?
lines.id: Oh, I see. And the class? Is it hard?
lines.literal: ah, I-understood. and the class? is(ser) difficult?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: A aula é ótima, mas eu estou perdido hoje.
lines.id: The class is great, but I'm lost today.
lines.literal: the class is(ser) great, but I I-am(estar) lost today.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Calma. O professor é muito paciente.
lines.id: Relax. The teacher is very patient.
lines.literal: calm. the teacher is(ser) very patient.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: É, mas ele está no Japão este mês.
lines.id: Yes, but he's in Japan this month.
lines.literal: is(ser), but he he-is(estar) in-the Japan this month.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sério? Então a aula está online?
lines.id: Really? So the class is online?
lines.literal: serious? then the class it-is(estar) online?

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Está, sim. Mas hoje ele está aqui!
lines.id: It is. But today he's here!
lines.literal: it-is(estar), yes. but today he he-is(estar) here!

notes: **Two verbs, one English "to be".** *Ele é brasileiro* and *ele está no Japão* both translate with "is" in English. The difference: the first says **who he is**, the second says **where he is right now**. English leaves that to context; Portuguese makes you choose in every sentence.

**Estar com — "to be with".** Portuguese doesn't say "I'm sleepy" but *estou com sono* = "I'm with sleep". This pattern covers nearly every physical state: *estou com fome* (hungry), *estou com sede* (thirsty), *estou com frio* (cold), *estou com pressa* (in a hurry), *estou com medo* (scared). Learn the pattern once, and twenty sentences come for free.

**Nossa!** is the most typically Brazilian exclamation. Literally "our (Lady)" — short for *Nossa Senhora* — but today it just means "gosh", "wow" or "oh my", for happy and sad surprises alike. You'll hear it dozens of times a day in Brazil.

**Repeating the verb to say "yes", again.** *Então a aula está online?* → *Está, sim.* Notice that what gets repeated is the verb **of the question**, so this time it's *está*, not *é*. This habit trains your ear to tell the two apart.

grammars.title: Estar — "to be (located); to be (right now)"
body: Its forms are as irregular as *ser*'s, and it's used just as often. Note that the first syllable (*es-*) is never stressed.
after: In everyday speech, Brazilians chop off the first syllable: *tô*, *tá*, *tamos*, *tão*. *Tudo bem?* → *Tá tudo bem!* These short forms aren't written in formal letters, but they're what you'll hear on the street, in series and in songs. *Tá?* on its own means "okay?", and *tá bom* means "okay, fine".
⚠️ The verb itself means "to be located" — so *estar* is also the one used for **places**: *Onde você está?* = "Where are you?", *O livro está na mesa* = "The book is on the table".

grammars.title: The dividing rule
body: The rule you'll find online — "ser for permanent, estar for temporary" — is right about eighty percent of the time and misleading the rest. The table below is more reliable because it sorts by **the type of information**, not by how long it lasts.
after: The fastest way to decide: ask yourself **"does this answer who/what it is, or how it is right now?"** The first is *ser*, the second *estar*.

⚠️ Look at the "place" row. Location is **always** *estar*, even for things that will never move: *O Rio de Janeiro está no Brasil* — though the city clearly isn't going anywhere. This is where "permanent versus temporary" falls apart, and "type of information" still stands.

grammars.title: When the wrong choice changes the meaning
body: Some adjectives can go with either verb, and the meaning shifts. This isn't an advanced subtlety — it's used every day.

rows: That soup is a good dish.

after: The second row is a practical reason to be careful: complimenting someone with *você está linda* means "you look gorgeous today", and that's a warm compliment. Saying *você é linda* to someone you've just met sounds a lot bolder than you might intend.

blocks.text: They all use *estar*, and they all change their ending when a woman is speaking. The forms given here are the masculine ones.

Notice that *feliz* and *triste* don't change for gender — they belong to the group of adjectives that don't care, like *grande* in unit 2. The rest do change: a woman says *estou cansad**a***, *estou ocupad**a***, *estou perdid**a***.

sections.title: Estar com — states English expresses with an adjective

blocks.text: The eight sentences below all use the same pattern, where English simply uses an adjective. Literally, it's always "I'm **with** something".

⚠️ Don't translate "I'm hungry" word for word as *estou faminto*. That form exists, but it sounds like you're writing a novel. What real Brazilians say is *estou com fome* — or, in the short form, ***tô com fome***.

Compare the weather, which does **not** use *com*: *Está frio hoje* = "It's cold today" (the weather), while *Estou com frio* = "I'm cold" (my body). The difference is the same as "it's cold" versus "I'm cold" in English.
Cover the Portuguese, read the English, and rebuild the Portuguese sentence from memory. Only then uncover it to check.

items: Hi! How are you? → *Oi! Tudo bem?*
My name is Budi. → *Eu me chamo Budi.*
I'm from Jakarta. → *Eu sou de Jacarta.*
